title: Congenital Immunodeficiency Diseases
subject: Immune System (IMMU)

overview.intro: This chapter covers five classic inborn immune defects: common variable immunodeficiency, DiGeorge syndrome, selective IgA deficiency, severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), and X-linked agammaglobulinemia. Each disease is explained from the developmental step that fails, so its infections, laboratory pattern, and associated findings follow from mechanism. The final section turns this into a method: read the infection pattern and the age of onset, name the defective arm of immunity (B cell, T cell, phagocyte, or complement), and choose the first test. Board questions usually present a child or adult with recurrent infections and expect exactly that chain of reasoning.
prerequisites: B cell development in the marrow, V(D)J recombination, and the pre-B cell receptor (IM-12)
T cell development and selection in the thymus
T cell help for B cells: CD40 ligand, cytokines, germinal centers, and class switching
Immunoglobulin classes, secretory IgA, and placental transfer of IgG
Complement pathways, opsonization, and the membrane attack complex

connections.how: Failed third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development explains the thymic and parathyroid defects of DiGeorge syndrome.
RAG, IL2RG, JAK3, and ADA defects define the SCID genotypes and their lymphocyte profiles.
NADPH oxidase and purine salvage explain chronic granulomatous disease and ADA-deficient SCID.

connections.to: Congenital heart disease and hypoparathyroidism (CV-14, EN-12-B)
connections.how: Neural crest and pharyngeal pouch defects link conotruncal anomalies and neonatal hypocalcemia to DiGeorge syndrome.

connections.to: Celiac disease and transfusion reactions (GI-11, HE-7)
connections.how: IgA deficiency causes falsely negative IgA celiac serology and anaphylactic transfusion reactions.

terms.def: An inherited or developmental defect of the immune system, as opposed to one acquired from infection, drugs, or protein loss.
A terminally differentiated B cell that secretes large amounts of a single antibody.
DNA recombination in activated B cells that replaces the IgM constant region with that of IgG, IgA, or IgE, driven by CD40 ligand and cytokines from helper T cells.
A mu heavy chain paired with a surrogate light chain whose signal, relayed through Bruton tyrosine kinase, lets a pre-B cell proliferate and mature.
The receptor subunit, encoded by IL2RG, shared by the receptors for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21.
T cell receptor excision circle, a piece of DNA cut out during T cell receptor gene rearrangement in the thymus, used as a marker of new T cell production.
The soft tissue density of the thymus in the anterior mediastinum on an infant chest radiograph.
Dimeric IgA joined by J chain and transported across mucosal epithelium by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor.
Bacteria with a polysaccharide capsule that resists phagocytosis until the organism is opsonized by antibody and complement.
A flow cytometry test of neutrophil oxidative burst in which reactive oxygen species convert dihydrorhodamine to fluorescent rhodamine.
A functional assay of the whole classical complement pathway, C1 through C9, measured by lysis of antibody-coated sheep red cells.
Attack on host tissues by viable donor T cells from a blood product that the recipient cannot reject.

blocks.text: Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is a group of disorders in which B cells are present, usually in normal numbers, but fail to complete the last stage of their development: activation in germinal centers, class switching, and differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells. The result is low IgG together with low IgA, low IgM, or both, and a poor antibody response to vaccines. It is the most frequent clinically significant primary antibody deficiency.

Marrow development is intact, so naive B cells reach the lymphoid follicles, but they respond poorly to antigen and T cell help. Few switched memory B cells and plasma cells form, and gut or marrow biopsies show scarce plasma cells. Variants in genes for B cell activation and survival (for example TACI, ICOS, CD19, and NFKB2) and in immune regulators (CTLA4, LRBA) explain only a minority of cases; most are sporadic with complex inheritance. Some patients also have T cell dysfunction.

With no single developmental block, the defect often appears late. Onset peaks in the second to fourth decades, although children are also affected, and men and women are affected equally. The classic patient is an adult with a normal early history who develops recurrent sinusitis, otitis, and pneumonia with encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. Repeated lower respiratory infection destroys bronchial walls and leaves bronchiectasis. Without mucosal IgA, Giardia persists in the small intestine and causes chronic diarrhea and malabsorption.

CVID is a disorder of immune regulation as well as deficiency. About a fifth or more of patients develop autoimmunity, most often immune thrombocytopenia and autoimmune hemolytic anemia; total IgG is low, but defective B cell selection and regulatory T cell function still allow a few self-reactive clones to make pathogenic autoantibody. Chronic immune activation causes lymphoid hyperplasia (splenomegaly, nodular lymphoid hyperplasia of the gut) and noncaseating granulomas in lung, liver, and lymph nodes that resemble sarcoidosis. The risk of B cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma is greatly increased, and gastric adenocarcinoma is also more common.

blocks.title: Laboratory pattern in CVID
rows: IgA low; IgM low in about half
Failed class switching and plasma cell differentiation
The block is after marrow development
blocks.caption: Diagnosis rests on low IgG with low IgA or IgM, poor vaccine responses, and exclusion of secondary causes such as protein loss or drugs.

blocks.predict: A 32-year-old woman with CVID has a negative IgG antibody test for an infection she clearly had last year. Is the infection excluded?
blocks.explain: No. She cannot reliably make specific antibody, so serology is falsely negative; infection must be shown directly by culture, antigen, or nucleic acid testing.
blocks.check: Compare with the vaccine response row of the laboratory table.

blocks.text: DiGeorge syndrome is the immunologic part of the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, the most common microdeletion syndrome in humans at about 1 in 4,000 live births. A segment of about 3 million base pairs is lost from one copy of chromosome 22, usually de novo, and passed on as an autosomal dominant trait when a parent carries it. The key gene for the pharyngeal features is TBX1, a T-box transcription factor; losing one copy disturbs the pharyngeal pouches and arches and the neural crest-derived tissue that fills them.

blocks.title: From 22q11.2 deletion to the clinical triad
steps: 22q11.2 deletion removes one copy of TBX1
Pharyngeal pouches, arches, and neural crest mesenchyme develop abnormally
Third pouch: thymus and inferior parathyroids hypoplastic
Fourth pouch: superior parathyroids hypoplastic
Neural crest: faulty aorticopulmonary septum and outflow tract
T cell lymphopenia, hypocalcemia, conotruncal heart defects
blocks.caption: One embryologic defect explains the immune, endocrine, and cardiac findings.

blocks.text: The thymus forms from third pouch endoderm, so a small thymus limits production of mature T cells. Most patients have partial DiGeorge syndrome, with low to near-normal T cell counts that often improve with age; less than about 1% have complete athymia, with almost no naive T cells and a course like SCID. When T cells are deficient, infections are those that T cells control: viruses, Candida and other fungi, and Pneumocystis. B cells are present and immunoglobulins are usually normal, although antibody responses can be weak without T cell help. The thymic shadow is small or absent on chest radiograph.

Absent or small parathyroids cause hypoparathyroidism. Low PTH reduces bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, phosphate excretion, and calcitriol synthesis, giving low calcium with high phosphate. Low ionized calcium makes nerve Na+ channels open more easily, so neuromuscular excitability rises; newborns present in the first days with tetany or seizures, and the QT interval lengthens.

Cardiac neural crest cells build the aorticopulmonary septum that divides the truncus arteriosus into aorta and pulmonary trunk. Faulty migration causes conotruncal defects: interrupted aortic arch type B, persistent truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot, and ventricular septal defects. Abnormal arch development produces the facies (hooded eyelids, low-set ears, short philtrum, small mandible) and cleft palate or velopharyngeal insufficiency. The CATCH-22 mnemonic (cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate, hypocalcemia, chromosome 22) collects these features. Learning difficulty and later psychiatric illness, including schizophrenia, are also more common. The deletion is confirmed by fluorescence in situ hybridization or chromosomal microarray.

Selective IgA deficiency is defined as serum IgA below about 7 mg/dL with normal IgG and IgM in a person older than 4 years, once other causes are excluded; the age limit exists because IgA normally rises slowly through childhood. It is the most common primary immunodeficiency, affecting about 1 in 300 to 700 people of European descent and fewer in East Asian populations. IgA-bearing B cells are present but fail to mature into IgA-secreting plasma cells. The cause is usually unknown, and it clusters in families with CVID, with which it shares susceptibility genes.

Most affected people are healthy because mucosal defense has a backup. Secretory IgA is a J chain-linked dimer carried across epithelium by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor; pentameric IgM also contains J chain and uses the same receptor, so secretory IgM partly takes its place. Symptomatic patients, often those with an accompanying IgG2 subclass deficiency or poor polysaccharide responses, have recurrent sinusitis, otitis, and bronchitis, and Giardia infection of the small bowel: the surfaces where IgA normally neutralizes microbes before they attach.

IgA deficiency is associated with atopy and with autoimmune disease, including systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, immune thrombocytopenia, and type 1 diabetes. The strongest link is celiac disease, in which IgA deficiency is about 10 to 15 times more common than in the general population. Reduced mucosal exclusion of food and microbial antigens is one proposed explanation, but the mechanism is not settled.

blocks.title: Anaphylactic transfusion reaction in IgA deficiency
steps: IgA never made, so no tolerance to IgA
Some patients form anti-IgA antibodies, mostly IgG
Transfused plasma or whole blood delivers donor IgA
Anti-IgA binds donor IgA; mast cell and complement mediators released
Bronchospasm, hypotension, and urticaria within minutes
blocks.caption: Anaphylaxis can occur during a first transfusion because sensitization needs no prior transfusion. Severe reactions are uncommon even among patients with anti-IgA.

blocks.text: Any serologic test that detects a patient's IgA antibody cannot be positive if no IgA is made, so the usual celiac screen, IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase, is falsely negative. Total IgA is therefore measured alongside it, and in IgA deficiency the IgG-based tests (IgG anti-deamidated gliadin peptide or IgG anti-tissue transglutaminase) are informative instead. IgA deficiency can also progress to CVID, so a falling IgG in a known patient is significant.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of genetic disorders in which T cell development fails. B cells need T cell help for class switching and for most antibody responses, so both arms of adaptive immunity are lost even when B cells are present. Incidence is about 1 in 50,000 to 60,000 births. Maternal IgG gives partial protection against bacteria for a few months, but nothing controls viruses, fungi, or Pneumocystis, so infants become ill within the first months of life.

blocks.title: Major SCID genotypes
rows: No IL-7 signal for thymocytes and no IL-15 signal for NK cells
Kinase that carries the common gamma chain signal
Loss of the IL-7 signal alone
No V(D)J recombination, so no T or B cell receptors
Toxic purine metabolites kill all lymphocytes
blocks.caption: X-linked IL2RG deficiency is historically the most common form. B cells present in IL2RG and JAK3 SCID still cannot make useful antibody.

blocks.title: How ADA deficiency kills lymphocytes
steps: ADA deficiency: deoxyadenosine and adenosine accumulate
Lymphocytes phosphorylate deoxyadenosine to dATP
dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase
Deoxynucleotide pools fall; DNA synthesis and repair fail
Developing T, B, and NK cells die
blocks.caption: Lymphocytes are vulnerable because they have high kinase activity that traps deoxyadenosine as dATP.

blocks.text: The typical infant has failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, persistent oral thrush, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and severe or prolonged respiratory viral infections. The chest radiograph lacks a thymic shadow, tonsils and lymph nodes are absent, and the absolute lymphocyte count is usually low. Maternal T cells that crossed the placenta can engraft and cause a rash resembling graft-versus-host disease. Newborn screening detects SCID before infection by measuring TRECs; few TRECs means few newly made T cells.

Live attenuated vaccines depend on the host to contain a weakened organism. In SCID, rotavirus vaccine causes chronic diarrhea, BCG causes disseminated mycobacterial infection, and oral polio, measles, and varicella vaccine strains can cause fatal disease. Cellular blood products contain viable donor T lymphocytes. A normal recipient rejects them, but an infant with SCID cannot, so donor T cells engraft, proliferate, and attack host skin, gut, liver, and marrow. This transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease causes rash, diarrhea, hepatitis, and pancytopenia and is usually fatal. Gamma irradiation damages lymphocyte DNA so donor T cells cannot proliferate, which is why irradiated products prevent it.

blocks.title: Worked example: two infants without a thymic shadow
blocks.text: Infant A, a 4-month-old boy, has thrush, Pneumocystis pneumonia, and diarrhea. CD3 T cells are nearly absent, B cells are present, NK cells are absent, and calcium is normal. Infant B, 5 days old, has a seizure; calcium is low, phosphate is high, an echocardiogram shows truncus arteriosus, and CD3 T cells are low but present. Both lack a thymic shadow, so the radiograph alone cannot separate them. Infant A has the T absent, B present, NK absent pattern of IL2RG or JAK3 SCID; in a boy, X-linked IL2RG is likeliest. Infant B has a pharyngeal pouch defect: thymus, parathyroids, and outflow tract fail together, which points to 22q11.2 deletion. Calcium, the heart, and the face distinguish DiGeorge syndrome from SCID.

blocks.predict: Will a 2-month-old boy with IL2RG SCID have normal serum IgG and a normal B cell count?
blocks.explain: Often yes for both. B cells develop without the common gamma chain, and IgG at 2 months is mostly maternal. IgA and IgM are low, and he cannot make specific antibody, because T cell help and IL-21 signaling are missing.
blocks.check: Compare with the IL2RG row of the genotype table.

blocks.text: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA) results from mutations in BTK on the long arm of the X chromosome, which encodes Bruton tyrosine kinase. In the marrow, pro-B cells rearrange heavy chain genes and become pre-B cells, which display the mu heavy chain with a surrogate light chain as the pre-B cell receptor. Signaling from this receptor, relayed through BTK, drives proliferation and progression to light chain rearrangement. Without BTK the signal is lost and development stops at the pre-B stage.

blocks.title: B cell development and where antibody deficiencies block it
steps: Stem cell to pro-B cell: heavy chain V(D)J rearrangement
Pre-B cell: pre-B cell receptor signals through BTK (XLA blocks here)
Immature, then mature naive B cell with surface IgM and IgD
Germinal center: T cell help drives class switching
Plasma cell secretes antibody (CVID and IgA deficiency block here)
blocks.caption: An early block removes B cells; a late block leaves B cells but no plasma cells.

blocks.text: Mature B cells are nearly absent from blood (CD19-positive cells usually under 2% of lymphocytes) and from lymphoid tissue, so there are no germinal centers and no plasma cells. All immunoglobulin classes are very low. Tonsils, adenoids, and lymph nodes are small or impalpable because B cell follicles make up much of their bulk. T cell number and function are normal. The disease is X-linked recessive, so patients are almost always boys, sometimes with affected maternal male relatives.

Maternal IgG, with a half-life of about 3 weeks, protects the infant for the first months, so infections begin after about 6 months as it is catabolized. The organisms are those that antibody controls. Encapsulated bacteria such as S pneumoniae and H influenzae type b resist phagocytosis until IgG and complement opsonize them, causing otitis, sinusitis, pneumonia, and bacteremia. Enteroviruses reach the central nervous system through the blood and are cleared mainly by neutralizing antibody, so echovirus can cause chronic meningoencephalitis and live oral polio vaccine can cause paralytic polio. Giardia persists without mucosal IgA, and Mycoplasma infections of joints and airways also occur.

blocks.title: Primary antibody deficiencies compared
rows: IgA B cell to IgA plasma cell
Either sex, any age; often silent
IgG low with low IgA and/or IgM
IgA very low; IgG and IgM normal
Celiac disease, anaphylaxis to IgA in blood products
blocks.caption: Low IgG with absent B cells means XLA; low IgG with B cells present means CVID.

blocks.text: A girl with the same picture suggests autosomal recessive agammaglobulinemia, for example from mu heavy chain defects. Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy, a delay in the infant's own IgG production, differs by normal B cell numbers and spontaneous recovery.

sections.title: Reading the infection pattern and choosing the first test

blocks.text: Each arm of immunity is essential against particular organisms, so the infection pattern identifies the arm that has failed. Antibody with complement opsonizes encapsulated bacteria, whose polysaccharide capsules otherwise block phagocytosis, and neutralizing antibody stops enteroviruses during their viremic spread. T cells kill virus-infected cells and activate macrophages through interferon gamma, controlling viruses, fungi such as Candida, Pneumocystis, and intracellular bacteria such as mycobacteria. Neutrophils kill bacteria and fungi with oxidants derived from superoxide made by NADPH oxidase. When the oxidase is absent, as in chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), a characteristic set of catalase-positive bacteria and fungi survive; the classic explanation is that catalase-negative bacteria supply their own peroxide while catalase-positive organisms destroy it. The membrane attack complex (C5b to C9) is uniquely important for lysing Neisseria.

Age at onset is the second clue. Antibody defects stay hidden until maternal IgG falls after about 6 months, and CVID often appears in adults. T cell and combined defects present in the first weeks to months, as do severe phagocyte defects. Delayed separation of the umbilical cord, infections without pus, and a very high neutrophil count point to leukocyte adhesion deficiency, a defect of neutrophil migration, rather than CGD.

blocks.title: Infection pattern, defective arm, and first test
rows: Encapsulated bacteria, enteroviruses, Giardia; sinopulmonary infections
Low for age; then vaccine titers and B cell count
Lymphocyte count and flow cytometry (CD3, CD4, CD8)
Both groups in an infant with failure to thrive
Flow cytometry for T, B, and NK cells
T cells nearly absent; B and NK depend on gene
S aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia cepacia, Nocardia, Aspergillus
No rise in fluorescence after stimulation
blocks.caption: The first test screens the suspected arm; specific gene, protein, or functional tests follow.

blocks.text: Each test measures function or cells directly. Quantitative immunoglobulins are compared with age-specific ranges, since normal infant values are far lower than adult ones. Flow cytometry counts cells by surface markers: CD3 for T cells, CD4 and CD8 subsets, CD19 or CD20 for B cells, and CD16 and CD56 for NK cells. In the DHR test, stimulated neutrophils oxidize dihydrorhodamine 123 to fluorescent rhodamine, so absent fluorescence means absent NADPH oxidase activity; it has replaced the nitroblue tetrazolium test. CH50 measures the serum dilution that lyses 50% of antibody-coated sheep red cells, which requires every classical component from C1 through C9, so loss of any one gives a very low or zero value.

blocks.title: Worked example: an 8-month-old boy with pneumonia
blocks.text: An 8-month-old boy has his third episode of otitis and now pneumococcal pneumonia. His tonsils cannot be seen, and a maternal uncle died of meningitis in childhood. Encapsulated bacteria point to the antibody arm, and onset after 6 months fits loss of maternal IgG, so the first test is quantitative immunoglobulins: IgG, IgA, and IgM are all very low. The next question is whether B cells exist. Flow cytometry shows CD19 B cells under 1% with normal CD3 T cells. Absent B cells, absent tonsils, a boy, and a maternal family history indicate XLA. Had B cells been normal in an adult, the diagnosis would be CVID.

blocks.predict: A 19-year-old has a second episode of meningococcal meningitis. Which arm is defective, which test comes first, and would a normal IgG level rule out an immunodeficiency?
blocks.explain: Terminal complement (C5 to C9), screened with CH50. A normal IgG does not rule it out, because the defect is the membrane attack complex that lyses Neisseria, not antibody production.
blocks.check: Compare with the first paragraph and the last row of the table.

integration.text: These diseases connect embryology, genetics, biochemistry, and immunology. DiGeorge syndrome is a pharyngeal pouch and neural crest defect that happens to remove the thymus, so its immune, endocrine, and cardiac findings share one origin. SCID genotypes map onto steps of lymphocyte development: cytokine signaling (IL2RG, JAK3), V(D)J recombination (RAG), and purine salvage (ADA). The antibody deficiencies sit along the B cell pathway, with XLA blocking early and CVID and IgA deficiency blocking late.

Pathology adds the paradox of immune dysregulation: CVID and IgA deficiency carry autoimmunity, and CVID carries lymphoma, because the same faults that reduce protective antibody also impair tolerance and lymphoid control. The infection-pattern method is a screening tool rather than a rule; organisms overlap, partial defects blur the categories, and secondary causes such as HIV infection, protein-losing states, and immunosuppressive drugs must be excluded before a defect is called primary.

summary: Antibody defects cause encapsulated bacterial, enteroviral, and Giardia infections and appear after about 6 months, when maternal IgG is gone.
XLA is a BTK defect that stops B cell development at the pre-B stage: boys with absent B cells, very low immunoglobulins, and scant tonsils.
CVID has B cells that fail to become plasma cells: low IgG with low IgA or IgM, usually adult onset, plus autoimmunity, granulomas, and lymphoma risk.
Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency; it is usually silent because secretory IgM compensates.
IgA deficiency causes falsely negative IgA celiac serology and, in patients with anti-IgA antibodies, anaphylaxis to IgA in blood products.
DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2, TBX1) disrupts the third and fourth pouches and neural crest: T cell lymphopenia, hypocalcemic tetany, conotruncal defects, abnormal facies, and cleft palate.
SCID removes T cell function and therefore antibody responses, causing thrush, Pneumocystis, viral infection, diarrhea, and failure to thrive in early infancy with no thymic shadow and low TRECs.
In SCID, live vaccines cause disseminated infection and nonirradiated cellular blood products cause transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.
Infection pattern to first test: antibody, quantitative immunoglobulins; T cell, flow cytometry; phagocyte, DHR; terminal complement, CH50.

verify: Prevalence figures (22q11.2 deletion about 1 in 4,000, SCID about 1 in 50,000 to 60,000, selective IgA deficiency about 1 in 300 to 700 in people of European descent) vary between sources and populations.
The IgA cutoff of about 7 mg/dL (0.07 g/L) and the age limit of 4 years follow common diagnostic criteria; confirm the values NABNE expects.
Proportions in CVID (autoimmunity in about a fifth or more, low IgM in about half) and the peak age of onset differ among cohorts.
The share of 22q11.2 deletion patients with complete athymia (less than about 1%) is an estimate; confirm if tested.
X-linked IL2RG is described as the most common SCID genotype in older series, but newborn screening data show a broader spread; confirm which NABNE expects.

The mechanism of anaphylactic transfusion reactions in IgA deficiency is attributed mainly to IgG anti-IgA with complement activation, with IgE anti-IgA in some patients; the relative roles are debated.
The relative increase of IgA deficiency in celiac disease (about 10 to 15 times) is a consensus estimate that varies by study.
Confirm whether NABNE accepts the CATCH-22 mnemonic; some current sources avoid it.
The threshold of CD19-positive cells under 2% for XLA follows common diagnostic criteria; confirm if tested.
The catalase explanation for CGD organisms is classic teaching that animal studies challenge; confirm the framing NABNE expects.
